Lackawanna Blues is a beautiful testament to their relationship, and the wider community surrounding it.

Ruben Santiago-Hudson summons a world of ghosts, or at least as many as will fill a couple boarding houses and a lifetime of gratitude, in his affectionate Lackawanna Blues, the one-man autobiographical tour through a childhood made golden by the presence of a strong and loving guardian angel.

The writing, which is more a series of scattered anecdotes and memories than a traditional narrative, mixes retelling the characters’ sorrowful pasts with lively comic touches, leading to earnest character portraits that are affecting and involving.
The miracle of this “Lackawanna Blues” is the absolute lack of effort Santiago
Lackawanna Blues is not to be missed.
What he does most masterfully is exorcising the graceful and benevolent ghost of a woman whose kindness in the face of racism and anger in the face of injustice are nothing short of radical.
He's a great writer, a great actor and a great director... But it is not a great show.

Yet, as engrossing as much of the show is -- and all of it is enhanced by the almost-constant background guitar-playing by Junior Mack of the music of the late, great Bill Sims Jr. -- I have to admit (somewhat sadly) that the piece didn’t fully satisfy me.
